unit.title: Assist in the provision of on the job training

summary: This unit prepares you to help train apprentices and new workers on an electrical crew. You will learn to find out what a trainee already knows, plan short training sessions with clear objectives, keep trainees safe, explain and demonstrate tasks, supervise practice, give useful feedback, check progress, keep honest training records, report to your supervisor and judge whether the training worked.

blocks.p: Most electricians learn the trade on the job, from the people they work beside. **On-the-job training (OJT)** means teaching real tasks in the workplace while the work gets done. This unit is for Level 3 electricians who are asked to help train apprentices, Level 2 trainees on work experience and new workers in their crew. You do not replace the formal course or the assessor: you help the trainee turn what they were taught into safe, skilled work.

blocks.h: What you must be able to do

head: Task
What it looks like on the job
rows: Explain your role and its limits
Say what a workplace trainer is responsible for, who else is involved and where your role ends.
Find out training needs
Compare what the trainee can do now with what the job needs, using records, questions and watching them work.
Plan and prepare training
Write clear objectives and a short plan, break tasks into steps with key points, and get the place, tools and materials ready.
Keep trainees safe
Give an induction, check PPE, keep trainees on dead work after safe isolation, supervise closely and stop unsafe acts.
Explain and demonstrate
Use plain words and a step-by-step demonstration, with the reasons for the key points.
Supervise practice
Watch closely, correct mistakes and build skill until the task is right every time.
Give feedback
Tell the trainee, soon and specifically, what went well and what to improve, and agree the next step.
Check progress
Watch the trainee do the task alone, ask questions and judge it against the standard.
Keep records and report
Fill in the logbook or training record honestly and tell your supervisor about progress and problems.
Evaluate the training
Find out whether the training worked and use what you learn to improve it.

blocks.h: Who is who in workplace training

head: Person or body
Role
rows: Trainee or apprentice
Learns the job; follows instructions and safety rules; keeps the logbook up to date; asks when unsure.
Workplace trainer (you)
Helps plan, demonstrates, supervises practice, gives feedback, records sessions and reports progress.
Supervisor or foreman
Agrees the training plan, decides who works where, deals with problems beyond your authority.
Training officer or coordinator
Organises the training programme for the firm or Centre and keeps the main records.
Assessor
A qualified person, meeting the training body's rules, who makes the **formal judgement** of competence for the qualification.
HEART/NSTA Trust
Jamaica's national training agency: it manages the NVQ-J and the apprenticeship programmes.
NCTVET
The National Council on Technical and Vocational Education and Training, which sets the standards and awards the NVQ-J certificates.

blocks.note: NVQ-J training is **competency-based**: each unit of competency says what a worker must be able to do and to what standard. A trainee is judged **competent** or **not yet competent (NYC)**; there are no marks out of 100 for a practical task. The unit standard is your guide to what the trainee must reach.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: Read the sections in order: they follow the training cycle from finding needs to evaluating the result. Then try the practice test and read every explanation. Your instructor will give you the forms you will use: training needs checklist, session plan, job breakdown sheet, observation sheet and logbook page.

flow: Find out the training needs
Plan and prepare the training
Deliver it: explain, demonstrate, supervise practice
Check progress and give feedback
Record and report
Evaluate and improve, then start again with the next need

ul: Helping to find out what the trainee can already do and what they need to learn.
Agreeing a training plan with your supervisor and the trainee.
Preparing tools, materials and a safe place to train.
Explaining and demonstrating each task, and supervising practice closely.
Keeping the trainee on safe, dead work and stopping any unsafe act at once.
Giving clear feedback and recording each session in the logbook or training record.
Reporting progress, and any problems, to the supervisor or training officer.
**You are not the assessor.** You may judge that a trainee is ready, but the formal decision that they are competent for the qualification is made by a qualified assessor.
You do not change the training plan, the site rules or the trainee's duties on your own; you agree changes with the supervisor.
You do not let a trainee do work that is beyond your own competence, or beyond what the supervisor has agreed.
Personal, welfare, attendance and discipline matters go to the supervisor or training officer.

blocks.p: Trainees copy what they see, including bad habits. If you skip proving your tester, leave your safety glasses on your head or leave offcuts on the floor, your trainee will too, however well you explain the rules. Work the way you want them to work, every time.

blocks.h: Ways of training on the job

head: Method
What it is
Good for
rows: Demonstration and practice
You show the task; the trainee practises under supervision.
Practical skills: terminations, bending conduit, safe isolation.
Coaching
Short, regular guidance while the trainee does real work.
Building speed and judgement on tasks already learnt.
Shadowing
The trainee follows an experienced worker to watch how the job is done.
The first days on a new kind of job; learning the routine and the site.
Mentoring
A longer-term relationship giving advice and support.
Confidence, career choices, professional habits.
Toolbox talks
Short talks on site about a hazard or method.
Safety reminders for the whole crew.
Job aids
Picture cards, checklists, sketches.
Trainees who find reading hard; complex sequences.

blocks.p: A **training needs analysis** finds the gap between what a worker can do now and what the job needs them to do. Train the gap: not what they already know, and not tasks they will not use.

flow: List the tasks the crew's work needs, using the units of competency and the coming jobs
Find out what the trainee can already do: records, talk, and watching dead tasks
Compare the two and list the gaps
Put the gaps in order: safety first, then the tasks coming up soonest
Agree the list with the supervisor and the trainee

blocks.h: Finding out what the trainee can do

head: Source
What it shows
Watch out
rows: Certificates and logbooks
What they have been taught and signed off for.
Being taught a task is not the same as doing it well on site.
Talking with the trainee
What they think they can do, what they feel unsure about, how they like to learn.
Some people overrate themselves; some underrate themselves.
Watching them do a few dead tasks
Their real skill, speed and safe habits.
Use a training board or isolated, proved-dead work.
Their previous supervisor or instructor
Strengths and weak spots.
Ask with the trainee's knowledge.

blocks.p: **Example.** A trainee bends PVC conduit well but makes untidy terminations at the panel. The need is clear: the next training should focus on terminations, not on conduit.

Some workers come with years of experience but no certificate. Check what they can do, have their skills assessed where the training body allows (HEART/NSTA Trust offers assessment of prior learning), and train only the gaps, such as the code, testing or paperwork. Making an experienced worker repeat everything wastes their time and loses their goodwill.

head: Preference
The trainee likes
Use
rows: Visual
Seeing: diagrams, pictures, demonstrations.
Sketches, picture cards, colour-coded diagrams, a clear demonstration.
Auditory
Hearing: explanations and discussion.
Talk through each step and its reason; let them say it back.
Kinaesthetic (hands-on)
Doing the task with their own hands.
Short explanations, then practice early and often.

blocks.note: Most people learn best from a **mix**: seeing it, hearing why, and doing it. Ask how a trainee likes to learn and lean towards it, but always show, explain and let them practise.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.h: Other needs to find out, kindly

ul: **Reading and writing.** Some trainees find reading hard and are embarrassed about it. Ask privately, and plan pictures, demonstrations and reading procedures aloud with them.
**Numbers.** Measuring, cable lengths and calculations may need extra practice.
**Language.** Explain trade words and check understanding.
**Confidence.** A shy trainee may not ask questions in front of the crew.
**Health or disability.** Anything that affects safe work, such as colour vision for identifying conductors, is discussed privately with the supervisor.

head: Task for the house-wiring crew
Can do already
Needs training
Priority
rows: Safe isolation: lock, tag, prove dead
Knows the steps
Proving the tester before and after, every time
1 (before any other work)
Fixing boxes level and at the right height
Yes
Drawing cable into conduit
Partly
Using draw wire and lubricant; not overfilling
Terminating outlets and switches
Partly
Strip lengths, tight terminals, ground connections
Reading the layout drawing
No
Symbols, scale, heights
Terminating at the panel
No
Later in the plan

blocks.p: A **learning objective** says what the trainee will be able to do at the end of the session. A good one has three parts: the **performance** (what they will do), the **conditions** (with what, where) and the **standard** (how well).

head: Weak objective
Better objective
rows: Understand safe isolation.
On the training board, isolate, lock off, tag and prove a circuit dead, with the tester proved before and after, in the correct order, without help.
Learn about drawings.
Using the layout drawing, mark every outlet and switch position in one apartment correctly, without help.
Know how to wire outlets.
Terminate three outlets on the training board with correct strip lengths, no bare copper showing and all terminals tight.

blocks.p: Words such as 'understand', 'know' and 'learn about' cannot be seen or measured. Use action words you can check: isolate, terminate, mark, measure, explain, test.

head: Part of the plan
Example
rows: Task
Terminating outlets.
Objective
As above, with the standard.
Trainer
Name of the electrician who will train.
When and where
Tuesday, 7:30 a.m., on the training board in the site store; then on the Flat 3 outlets on Wednesday.
Method
Explain, demonstrate, supervised practice, then real work.
Resources
Training board, outlets, cable offcuts, screwdrivers, strippers, picture cards.
How it will be checked
Watched doing three outlets alone; questions on key points.
Record
Logbook entry signed by trainer and trainee.

ul: **Safety first:** safe isolation before any wiring task.
**Simple to complex**, so each skill builds on the last: fixing boxes, then drawing in cable, then terminating outlets, then the panel.
**Follow the job:** plan training around the tasks the crew has coming up, so the trainee practises real work in real site conditions soon after learning it.
**Little and often:** short sessions with practice in between are better than one long lecture.

blocks.p: A **job breakdown** (task breakdown) lists the steps of a task in order. For each step, write the **key points**: the details that make it safe, right or easier, and the reason for each. Teach a long task a few steps at a time.

head: Step: terminating a 110 V outlet (training board, no supply)
Key point
Reason
rows: 1. Confirm the board is isolated and proved dead, or is never connected
Treat it as live until proved dead
Builds the habit that saves lives on site.
2. Strip the outer sheath
Leave the sheath just inside the box
Protects the conductors where they enter.
3. Strip the conductor insulation
Use the strip gauge on the outlet
Too long leaves bare copper; too short gives a poor connection.
4. Form a hook and fit it under the screw
Hook clockwise
Tightening the screw pulls the hook in instead of pushing it out.
5. Connect the conductors
Hot (black) to the brass screw, neutral (white) to the silver screw, ground (green or bare) to the green screw
Correct polarity and a working ground.
6. Tighten the terminals
To the maker's torque
Loose terminals overheat and cause fires.
7. Fold the conductors in and fix the outlet level
No conductor trapped or strained
Prevents damage and a crooked finish.
8. Check before anyone energises it
Ground continuity and polarity checked; energising only by the authorised person
Faults are found while it is safe.

ul: **The place:** quiet, safe, well lit, where the trainee can see and hear you. On a busy site, pick a corner away from noise and traffic, or arrange for noisy work to pause.
**Tools and instruments:** checked before the session. A faulty tester or a damaged screwdriver can harm the trainee and teaches bad habits.
**Materials and aids:** enough for practice; picture cards, drawings and the job breakdown sheet.
**A dead training board** for first practice, never connected to a supply.
**Agreement:** the plan agreed with your supervisor and explained to the trainee, so everyone knows what will be learnt, when and with whom.

head: Time
Activity
rows: 5 minutes
Put the trainee at ease; state the objective; ask what they already know.
10 minutes
Explain the task, the tools and why each key point matters.
10 minutes
Demonstrate at normal speed, then slowly, step by step.
25 minutes
Trainee practises while you watch and coach.
10 minutes
Questions to check understanding; feedback; logbook entry.

blocks.p: A trainee does not yet see hazards the way you do. While they are in your care, their safety is your first job.

head: Rule
What it means in practice
rows: Dead work only
Trainees work only on circuits that have been isolated, locked off and proved dead, under supervision. Never live work, never live testing alone.
Their own lock and tag
When the crew isolates a circuit, the trainee fits their own padlock and tag, so nobody can switch it on while they work on it.
Close supervision
Keep the number of trainees per supervisor small, so each one can be watched and helped.
Induction on day one
Site hazards, the emergency procedure, the alarm, the assembly point, first aid, welfare and site rules.
PPE checked
Safety boots, hard hat, eye protection, gloves for the task; worn properly; damaged items replaced.
Tools and power tools
Checked before use; trainees shown how to use them before using them; guards in place.
Work at height
Ladders and towers inspected and set up correctly; trainees not left alone at height.
Heat and hydration
Water, shade and rest breaks; hot roof spaces worked early in the day.

blocks.h: Safe isolation, as you teach it

flow: Identify the circuit from the drawings and schedule, and test, do not trust labels
Switch off at the breaker or isolator
Lock off with your own padlock and keep the key
Fit a danger tag with your name and the date
Prove the tester on a proving unit
Test between all conductors at the point of work
Prove the tester again on the proving unit
Only then start work

blocks.note: Teach the reason with every step: a tester with a flat battery or a broken lead can show 'dead' on a live circuit. Proving it before and after is the only way to know the reading is true.
blocks.label: Safety

ul: Built to the maker's instructions and inspected; standing level on firm ground; castor brakes on.
Guard rails and toe boards fitted at the working platform; outriggers fitted where required.
Never move a tower with anyone on it, stand on guard rails or rest a ladder against it.
If a trainee is about to climb a tower without guard rails, stop them and have it put right first.
Ladders: fibreglass for electrical work, about 1 out for every 4 up, three points of contact, never over-reach.

blocks.p: Roof spaces and enclosed rooms in Jamaica can be much hotter than outside by midday. Plan roof-space work for the early morning, in short spells, with water, rest and ventilation, and always with a second person nearby.

head: Condition
Signs
What to do
rows: Heat exhaustion
Heavy sweating, dizziness, headache, nausea, weakness, cramps.
Stop work, move them somewhere cool and shaded, loosen clothing, give water to sip, cool with wet cloths; get first aid and watch them.
Heat stroke (an emergency)
Confusion, collapse, hot skin, possibly no sweating, fits.
Call 110 at once; cool them fast with water and fanning while you wait; do not give drinks if they are not fully conscious.

flow: Stop the act at once, calmly
Make the situation safe
Explain the danger and why the rule exists
Show the safe way and have the trainee do it
Record it, and report it if it is serious or repeated

head: Step
What you do
rows: 1. Prepare the trainee
Put them at ease, say what the task is and why it matters, and find out what they already know.
2. Present the task
Explain, then demonstrate one step at a time, stressing each key point and its reason.
3. Try it out
The trainee does the task while you watch, explaining the key points as they go; you correct errors.
4. Follow up
Check often at first, encourage questions, then supervise less as they become reliable.

blocks.p: Many trainers remember it as **explain, demonstrate, practise, check**.

ul: Stand the trainee **beside you**, seeing the work from the side they will work from, not opposite you, where everything looks reversed.
Do the task once at **normal speed**, so they see the whole job, then again **slowly**, step by step, saying each step aloud.
Give the **reason** for each key point, such as sleeving a bare ground conductor or forming a clockwise hook. Knowing why helps them remember and apply it in new situations.
Split a long task into small groups of steps and teach each group before moving on. Most people can hold only a few new steps in mind at once.
Use the same tools and materials the trainee will use, and do it exactly the way you want it done.

blocks.p: Explain every trade word the first time you use it: 'CPC', 'EGC', 'prove dead', 'strapper', 'first fix'. A trainee who does not know a word may guess wrongly and be too shy to ask. Use pictures, sketches and the real part.

head: Type
Example
Use
rows: Open
'Why do we check the tester again after the test?'
Makes the trainee explain; checks understanding.
Closed
'Is this the neutral?'
Checks one fact quickly.
Probing
'What would you look at next?'
Takes a good answer further.
What if
'What could happen if the tester failed during your test?'
Makes them apply the idea to a new situation.

ul: 'Do you understand?' is a poor check: most trainees say yes to avoid looking foolish. Ask them to **explain in their own words or show the next step** instead.
Ask, pause to give thinking time, then invite the answer.
If an answer is wrong, thank them for trying, give a clue or rephrase, and help them reach the right answer. Correct the idea, not the person.
Never mock a wrong answer in front of the crew: trainees who are embarrassed stop answering, and stop asking.

head: Trainee
What helps
rows: Finds reading hard
Speak privately and kindly; rely more on showing and doing; picture cards and photos of each step; read procedures aloud with them; check understanding by watching and by open questions.
Learns best by watching
A clear demonstration, sketches and colour-coded diagrams.
Wants to get hands-on at once
A short explanation and demonstration first, then practice straight away, with you close by.
Shy or quiet
Chances to ask questions one-to-one; praise for good questions.
Hard of hearing or in a noisy place
Face them, move somewhere quieter, use gestures and written key points.

ul: Watch closely at first, and step in **at once** before any unsafe act.
On a dead training board, where there is no danger, let the trainee check their own work against the key points before you point out a mistake: finding errors is a skill they will need.
Every mistake is put right before they move on.
Let them practise several times, until the task is right **every time**, not just once.
Then practise in real site conditions, still supervised, and reduce supervision as they become reliable.

blocks.h: Common mistakes and how to correct them

head: Mistake
Why it matters
Correction
rows: Nicked conductor insulation when stripping
A weak spot that can fail and short later.
Point it out, cut back to good cable and remake it; show the right stripper setting.
Loose terminal
Overheats, scorches and can start a fire.
Show how to tighten to the maker's torque and check with a gentle tug.
Bare copper showing beyond the terminal
Can touch other parts or be touched.
Use the strip gauge; remake it.
Ground conductor left off or not sleeved
Metal parts may stay live in a fault.
Explain what the ground does; connect and sleeve it.
Hot and neutral reversed
Switches and fuses end up in the neutral; parts stay live when 'off'.
Remake; teach the colour and screw rules and the polarity test.
Skipping a step of safe isolation
Can kill.
Stop at once and deal with it as below.

blocks.h: A trainee who keeps taking a shortcut

flow: Stop the work at once and speak to them privately and calmly
Explain the danger plainly, for example a faulty tester showing dead on a live circuit
Ask why they skip it: there may be a reason, such as no proving unit in the kit or feeling rushed
Demonstrate again and have them repeat the full procedure correctly
Record what happened and the extra training given
If it happens again, report to the supervisor; they do no isolation work until they follow the procedure every time

blocks.p: **Feedback** tells the trainee how well they did and what to improve. Good feedback is:

ul: **Timely:** soon after the task, while it is fresh; the same day.
**Specific:** 'every terminal is tight and the ground is sleeved', not just 'good job'.
**About the work, not the person:** 'this joint is loose', not 'you are careless'.
**Balanced:** what went well, then one or two things to improve, with the reasons.
**Private** when it includes criticism.
**Two-way:** ask the trainee how they think it went first; this teaches them to judge their own work.
**Forward-looking:** agree the next step, then record it.

blocks.p: **Example.** 'How do you think that went? … Your cable runs are neat and every terminal is tight, well done. Two things: one neutral is not in the same order as its breaker, which makes fault-finding harder, and one ground is not sleeved. Let's put those right, then you do the next board on your own.'
Tell trainees when they do well: praise builds confidence and keeps them trying. Make it honest and specific, so it means something. Pass good reports on to the supervisor too.

Every trainee gets the same chances, respect and standard of training, whatever their sex, parish, background, religion or how they speak. No favourites, no nicknames that hurt, no jokes about anyone's background, and no harassment. A woman in an all-male crew, or a trainee from out of town, must feel safe to ask questions. If you see unfair treatment, stop it and report it.

head: Method
What you do
rows: Observation
Watch the trainee do the whole task alone, without help or reminders, on dead work or a training board.
Questioning
Ask open and 'what if' questions to check they know why each step matters and what to do if something goes wrong.
The finished work
Inspect it against the standard: neat, tight, correct, tested.
Records
Logbook entries, inspection results, call-backs on their work.

blocks.p: Check against the standard for the task: the unit of competency or the job procedure. One correct attempt, especially with help, is not enough. Look for the task done right **on their own, more than once, on different days or jobs**, so you know it was not luck.

head: Evidence must be
Meaning
rows: Valid
It shows the actual skill in the standard, not something else.
Sufficient
There is enough of it, over enough occasions.
Authentic
It is the trainee's own work.
Current
It shows what they can do now, not years ago.

blocks.p: A trainee who meets the standard safely and consistently is **competent** in that task. One who does not yet is **not yet competent (NYC)**: record what still needs work and plan more practice. NYC is not a failure; it is a step in the training. For the qualification, the formal decision is the assessor's.
Record each session in the trainee's **logbook** or training record. It shows what was learnt, when and who checked it, and it is evidence for the trainee's qualification.

ul: Date and place
The task and the objective
What was done, and the standard reached (for example 'three outlets terminated alone, all correct')
What still needs practice and the next step
The signatures of the trainer and the trainee

blocks.note: Every entry must be true. Never back-date entries or fill gaps from memory to make a logbook look complete; add only what you can confirm from job records, dated honestly. A logbook with invented entries is worthless as evidence.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Training records hold personal information about a trainee's progress and difficulties. Keep them secure, and share them only with those who need them: the trainee, the supervisor, the training officer and the assessor.

head: Tell the supervisor or training officer about
Why
rows: Good progress and tasks completed
So the plan moves on and the trainee gets credit.
A trainee falling behind the plan
So extra training or a change of plan can be agreed early.
A trainee still unsafe after several sessions
So extra training is agreed and they are kept off that task until safe.
Attendance, welfare or personal problems
These are beyond your role.
Unsafe acts that are serious or repeated
So they are dealt with formally.

flow: Ask the trainee how they think they are doing
Go through the plan and the logbook together
Give specific feedback: strengths and gaps
Agree the next steps and dates
Record and sign; tell the supervisor

blocks.p: Evaluation asks: did the training work, and how can it be better next time? Look at it from four levels, from how the trainee felt to what it did for the firm.

head: Level
Question
Electrical example of evidence
rows: 1. Reaction
Did the trainees find it clear and useful?
Comments at the end of a session; a short feedback form.
2. Learning
Can they now do the task?
Watched isolating and proving dead alone, correctly, on two occasions.
3. Behaviour on the job
Do they work this way on site, without reminders?
Supervisor sees them prove the tester before and after on every job.
4. Results
Has the work improved?
More of their work passes inspection first time; fewer call-backs; no near misses.

blocks.p: Each level tells you something different. Trainees can enjoy a session (level 1) and still not be able to do the task (level 2). The strongest evidence that training paid off comes from the job itself (levels 3 and 4).

ul: Check each objective in the training plan: can the trainee now do it to the standard?
Ask the trainee what helped them learn, what was hard and what could be better. Make it easy for them to be honest, privately if need be.
Ask the supervisor and the crew what they see on the job.
Look at work results: first-time inspection passes, call-backs, safe working.
Compare what was planned with what happened: tasks that took longer to learn, methods that did not work.
Change the next training: for example more practice time, more pictures and fewer written notes, slower demonstrations in smaller steps, or a quieter place to demonstrate.
Act on comments that show a trainee felt unable to ask questions or was treated unfairly.
Report the results to the supervisor and agree changes to the training plan.
Improve your own training: ask for feedback on how you train, as well as on what the trainee learnt.

blocks.p: Tick each statement only when you can do it without looking at the notes.

ul: I can explain the role of a workplace trainer, who else is involved, and why the formal assessment belongs to the assessor.
I can describe the training cycle and the main methods of on-the-job training.
I can carry out a training needs analysis and write the gaps in order of priority.
I can take account of prior learning, learning preferences and needs such as reading difficulties, sensitively.
I can write a learning objective with a performance, conditions and a standard.
I can write a training plan and a job breakdown with key points and reasons.
I can prepare a safe place, checked tools and a dead training board for a session.
I can keep trainees safe: induction, PPE, dead work only, their own lock and tag, close supervision, towers, ladders and heat.
I can teach safe isolation in the correct order, with the reason for proving the tester before and after.
I can use the four-step method and demonstrate a task so the trainee can see and follow it.
I can use open and 'what if' questions to check understanding instead of asking 'Do you understand?'.
I can supervise practice, correct common mistakes and deal with a trainee who takes shortcuts.
I can give timely, specific feedback about the work and agree the next step.
I can check progress by observation, questioning and the finished work, and decide competent or not yet competent.
I can complete an honest training record, keep it confidential and report progress and problems.
I can evaluate training at the four levels and use the results to improve it.

terms: Assessor
A qualified person who makes the formal judgement of a trainee's competence for the qualification.
Competent
Able to do a task safely, to the required standard, every time.
Competency-based training
Training and assessment against what a worker must be able to do, as set out in units of competency.
Demonstration
The part of a session in which the trainer shows how the task is done while the trainee watches.
Feedback
Telling a trainee how well they did and what to improve.
HEART/NSTA Trust
Jamaica's national training agency, which manages the NVQ-J and apprenticeship programmes.
Job (task) breakdown
A task split into small steps, in order, with key points and reasons, so each step can be taught in turn.
Key point
A detail in a step that makes it safe, right or easier.
Kinaesthetic
Learning best by doing the task with your own hands.
Learning objective
A statement of what the trainee will be able to do at the end of a session, under what conditions and to what standard.
Logbook
The record in which a trainee's practical tasks are listed and signed off.
Mentoring
Longer-term advice and support from an experienced worker.
Not yet competent (NYC)
The result given when a trainee has not yet reached the standard.
On-the-job training (OJT)
Teaching real tasks in the workplace while the work gets done.
Open question
A question that cannot be answered with yes or no, so the trainee must explain.
Shadowing
A new worker following an experienced worker to watch how the job is done.
Training needs analysis
Finding the gap between what a worker can do now and what the job needs.
Visual learner
Someone who learns best from diagrams, pictures and demonstrations.

c1.title: A new apprentice in Ewarton
c1.text: Desmond Walker, a Level 3 electrician, has been asked to help train Tevin Grant, 18, who has just joined the crew as an apprentice. The crew is wiring a block of six apartments in Ewarton, St Catherine. Tevin has a Level 2 certificate in Electrical Installation from a HEART/NSTA Trust centre and says he has 'done all of it'. On his first day Desmond sees that Tevin's terminations are neat, but he cannot find the outlet positions on the layout drawing. Desmond's supervisor wants a two-week training plan by Friday.

c2.title: A GFCI lesson in Annotto Bay
c2.text: At a contractor's training workshop in Annotto Bay, St Mary, Simone Reid will teach two apprentices, Jodi and Ricardo, to wire a GFCI outlet with LINE and LOAD terminals on a training board that is never connected to a supply. Jodi says she learns best from pictures and watching; Ricardo likes to get his hands on the job straight away. During his practice, Ricardo connects the incoming cable to the LOAD terminals.

c3.title: Summer work at a school in Porus
c3.text: Kemar Lewis is supervising two trainees at a primary school in Porus, Manchester, during the summer holidays. Damion is pulling cable through the roof space, and it is nearly midday. Shanique is about to fix a light in the hall from a mobile tower. Damion offers to 'quickly' change a faulty breaker in the school's live panel to save time, saying he has watched it done before.

c4.title: A progress review in Constant Spring
c4.text: Marcia Fraser, a workplace trainer at a contractor in Constant Spring, St Andrew, is reviewing apprentice Jevaughn Brown's progress after six weeks. His logbook has entries for only two of the six weeks. He has isolated a circuit correctly once, with Marcia prompting him. When she asks, 'Do you understand why we prove the tester before and after?', he says, 'Yes, miss.' Last week he fitted a ceiling fan on the training rig: his connections were neat and tight, but he hung the fan from an ordinary light box that is not rated to carry a fan.

c5.title: Three months of training in St Ann's Bay
c5.text: A contractor in St Ann's Bay has given on-the-job training to four apprentices for three months, led by workplace trainer Wayne Dixon. The manager, Mrs Grace Edwards, asks whether it has been worth the crew's time. Wayne has the apprentices' logbooks, the supervisor's inspection results, end-of-session feedback forms and the apprentices' comments. One apprentice, Nicole, wrote that the demonstrations were too fast and that she was afraid to ask questions in front of the men in the crew.

questions.q: Tevin says he has 'done all of it'. How should Desmond find out what he can really do?
o: Accept his word, since he already holds a Level 2 certificate in it
Watch him do some dead tasks and check his records against the job
Give him a written test on the wiring code before he does any work
Put him straight onto the apartment work and see what goes wrong
questions.why: A training needs analysis compares what the trainee can actually do with what the job needs. His certificate and logbook show what he was taught; watching him do a few dead tasks shows his real skill and how safely he works. The gap becomes his training plan.

questions.q: Which is the best-written objective for Tevin's first session on the layout drawing?
o: Tevin will understand electrical drawings much better than before
Tevin will look at a good range of drawings over the next two weeks
Desmond will explain all of the symbols used on the drawings to Tevin
Mark every outlet and switch in Flat 2 from drawing E-3, without help
questions.why: A good objective says what the trainee will do (mark the positions), under what conditions (from drawing E-3) and to what standard (every one, without help), so it can be checked. 'Understand' cannot be seen or measured, and an objective is about what the trainee does, not the trainer.

questions.q: Which order of training suits Tevin and the apartment job best?
o: Fixing boxes, then drawing in cable, then outlets, then the panel
Start with the panel, as it is the hardest and most important part
Terminating outlets first, then fixing boxes, then drawing in cable
Whatever the crew happens to be doing each day, in no special order
questions.why: Training builds from simple to harder tasks and follows the order of the real work, so each skill is used in the next and Tevin practises on real tasks as they come up. Starting with the panel, the most complex and highest-risk work, or training in a random order, makes learning slower and less safe.

questions.q: Which key point, with its reason, should Simone stress during the demonstration?
o: LINE and LOAD can be swapped freely, as the GFCI works either way
Only LOAD is used; the LINE terminals are for the maker's own tests
The ground wire is left off, as the GFCI protects people by itself
Supply goes on LINE; the LOAD side protects outlets further along
questions.why: The incoming supply must go to the LINE terminals; anything wired from LOAD is then protected as well. Reversed, the GFCI may not reset or may leave the outlet unprotected, which is why the key point is taught with its reason. A GFCI never replaces the equipment grounding conductor.

questions.q: How can Simone best suit both Jodi and Ricardo?
o: Let Ricardo wire it first unaided, then show Jodi what he did wrong
Give both a written handout and let them work it out on their own
Use picture cards and a demonstration, then let each practise soon
Teach Jodi today and Ricardo another day, each in a different way
questions.why: Most people learn best from a mix of seeing, hearing why and doing. Picture cards and a clear demonstration help Jodi, and practice straight after helps Ricardo. Letting a trainee wire it unaided before seeing it done teaches mistakes.

questions.q: Ricardo has connected the incoming cable to the LOAD terminals on the dead training board. What should Simone do?
o: Ask him to check his work against the key points and find the error
Say nothing, and let him find out when he fits one on a real job
Take the screwdriver and rewire it for him so that it is done right
Tell Jodi about his mistake so that she does not make the same one
questions.why: The board is never connected, so there is no danger, and asking him to check his own work against the key points teaches him to find mistakes himself, a skill he needs on site. The error must still be found and corrected before he moves on. Rewiring it for him teaches nothing.

questions.q: How should Kemar respond to Damion's offer to change the breaker in the live panel?
o: Let him do it, if he wears rubber gloves and uses insulated tools
Let him do it, as long as Kemar watches him closely all the time
Stop him: trainees work only on dead circuits, after isolation
Let him try, since he has watched it being done before by others
questions.why: A trainee must never work on live equipment. Changing a breaker means isolating the panel, locking off and proving dead, done or closely supervised by an authorised person and planned with the school. Gloves, insulated tools and watching do not make live work safe for a trainee.

questions.q: Which change to the plan would best protect the trainees from the heat in the roof space?
o: Let them work through lunch so they get out of the roof space sooner
Do roof-space work early in the morning, in short spells, with water
Give them salt tablets and let them carry on through the afternoon
Tell them to take off their shirts and boots to keep cool up there
questions.why: By midday a roof space can be far hotter than outside. Doing that work early in the day, in short spells with rest, water and ventilation where possible, prevents heat exhaustion. Working through breaks or removing PPE adds other dangers.

questions.q: Before Shanique climbs the mobile tower, what must Kemar check?
o: That she has a ladder ready to lean on the tower to reach higher
That someone is ready to push the tower along while she works on top
Brakes on, guard rails and toe boards fitted, and the tower level
That the tower is tall enough for her to stand on the guard rail
questions.why: A mobile tower must be built to the maker's instructions and inspected, standing level on firm ground, with the castor brakes on and guard rails and toe boards at the working platform. Never move it with anyone on it, stand on the guard rails or lean a ladder against it.

questions.q: How should Marcia check whether Jevaughn really knows why the tester is proved before and after?
o: Ask: 'What could happen if the tester failed during your test?'
Ask again, more firmly: 'Are you sure you understand it, Jevaughn?'
Accept his answer, since he has said yes and seems confident
Give him a page of notes on safe isolation to read at home
questions.why: A 'what if' question makes him use the idea: a tester that fails during the test could show 'dead' on a live circuit, which is why it is proved before and after. 'Yes' to 'Do you understand?' tells you little; trainees often say yes to avoid looking foolish.

questions.q: Jevaughn asks Marcia to record him as competent in safe isolation so he can move on. What should she do?
o: Record it, as he has completed the task correctly once with her help
Record it, so that he stays keen and does not lose heart in training
Not yet: he must do it correctly on his own on several occasions
Record it for all of his tasks now, to save time later in the year
questions.why: Competence means doing the task safely, to the standard, on your own, every time. Once with prompting is not enough evidence; Marcia should watch him do it alone on different occasions and record what she sees. For the qualification, the final decision is the assessor's.

questions.q: What should Marcia do about the four weeks with no logbook entries?
o: Fill in the missing weeks from memory, with dates to match the plan
Add only what job records confirm, dated honestly, and keep it up
Leave the gaps, as the logbook does not count towards his qualification
Ask Jevaughn to write the missing entries himself and sign them for her
questions.why: The logbook is evidence of what was learnt, when and who checked it, so every entry must be true. Gaps can be filled only from records that confirm the work, with honest dates, and sessions are recorded promptly from now on. Invented entries make the whole record worthless.

questions.q: Which feedback should Marcia give Jevaughn about the ceiling fan?
o: Good work, Jevaughn, well done; keep going exactly the way you are
That box is wrong again; you never think about what you are doing
Fine overall; I will change the box for you later when you have gone
Neat, tight joints; next, use a fan-rated box, because of the weight
questions.why: Useful feedback names exactly what went well, then one clear improvement with its reason: a fan's weight and wobble can pull an ordinary light box loose, so the code requires a box rated for fan support. Vague praise teaches nothing, criticising the person hurts confidence, and fixing it behind his back hides the lesson.

questions.q: Which evidence best shows Mrs Edwards that the training has improved the work on site?
o: The apprentices all said that they enjoyed the training sessions
The training corner has been painted and has new benches in it
Wayne spent more than 100 hours on the training in three months
More of the apprentices' work now passes inspection first time
questions.why: The question is whether the training changed the work, so the best evidence comes from the job: more work passing inspection first time, fewer call-backs, safe working without reminders. Enjoyment and hours spent matter, but they do not show a result.

questions.q: What should Wayne change because of Nicole's comment?
o: Slow down, break demonstrations into steps and make it safe to ask
Nothing, since the other three apprentices did not complain about it
Tell Nicole that she must speak up more if she wants to learn the job
Move Nicole to office work, where she will not need to ask questions
questions.why: A trainee's view shows how the training felt from the receiving end. Slower demonstrations in small steps, chances to ask questions privately and a crew that treats every trainee with respect help everyone, not only Nicole. Fair treatment means the same chances for women and men.

questions.q: What do the end-of-session feedback forms mainly tell Wayne?
o: Whether each apprentice is now fully competent in the task taught
How much the training has saved the firm in money this year
How the apprentices felt about each session, not what they can do
Which apprentices should be removed from the apprenticeship
questions.why: End-of-session forms measure reaction: whether the trainees found the session clear and useful. That helps improve the training, but learning, behaviour on the job and results for the firm must be checked in other ways, such as observation and inspection results.

questions.q: A new worker has wired houses for five years but has no certificate. What should his training plan do?
o: Have his skills checked and assessed, then train only the gaps
Start him on the full course from the beginning, like any new trainee
Assume he knows everything, since five years is plenty of experience
Give him only labouring duties until he can show a certificate
questions.why: Prior learning counts. Checking what he can already do, and having it assessed for the qualification where the training body allows, avoids wasting his time; training then covers only the gaps, such as the code or testing. Assuming nothing, or everything, is not a needs analysis.

questions.q: A trainee gives a wrong answer to your question in front of the crew. What is the best response?
o: Tell the crew the right answer and move straight on to the next one
Thank him, give a clue and help him reach the right answer
Point out the mistake firmly, so that everyone will remember it
Ask him the same question again until he gets it right
questions.why: Trainees stop answering if a wrong answer brings embarrassment. Acknowledge the attempt, give a clue or rephrase, and guide him to the right answer, so he learns and stays willing to try. Correct the idea, not the person.

questions.q: On a job breakdown sheet, what is a 'key point'?
o: The step that takes the longest time to do in the whole of the task
A detail in a step that makes it safe or right, with its reason
The name of the tool that is used for each step of the task
The last step of the task, where the finished work is checked
questions.why: A job breakdown lists the steps in order; the key points are what make each step safe, right or easier, such as 'use the strip gauge so no bare copper shows', with the reason. Teaching key points with reasons helps the trainee remember and apply them.

questions.q: A crew member asks to read an apprentice's training record and progress notes. What should you do?
o: Let him read it, since the whole crew works closely together
Pin the progress notes on the canteen board for everyone
Give him a copy, as long as he promises not to tell anyone
Share it only with those who need it, such as the supervisor
questions.why: Training records hold personal information about a trainee's progress and difficulties. They are kept secure and shared only with people who need them: the trainee, the supervisor, the training officer and the assessor.
